extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (real analysis / advanced calculus)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, definitions, and tests for determining convergence of improper Riemann integrals, related series tests (integral test), principal value, and basic facts about sequences of functions (pointwise vs uniform convergence) and when limits may be interchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: improper integral for nonnegative f on [a,∞)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : [a,∞) → ℝ is nonnegative and Riemann integrable on [a,b] for all b>a, then define ∫_a^∞ f = sup_{x ≥ a} ∫_a^x f. (The supremum may be infinite; in that case the integral diverges to +∞.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a monotone definition: x ↦ ∫_a^x f is increasing. Convergence is interpreted as the supremum being finite. Example/usage: used as the basic definition of an improper integral with an infinite endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential criterion for improper integral (tail-sequence test)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f as above, if {x_n}_{n=1}^∞ is any sequence with x_n → ∞, then ∫_a^∞ f converges iff the sequence ∫_a^{x_n} f has a (finite) limit; in that case the limit equals the value of the improper integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any sequence x_n → ∞ may be used to test convergence; the limit obtained (if exists) is independent of the particular sequence. This is used in proofs by showing Cauchy-ness of the tail integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test for improper integrals (nonnegative case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f,g : [a,∞) → ℝ be Riemann integrable on every [a,b] and suppose 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x≥a. If ∫_a^∞ g converges then ∫_a^∞ f converges. Conversely, if ∫_a^∞ f diverges to ∞, then ∫_a^∞ g diverges to ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity of the partial integrals and Cauchy criterion. Practical use: bound a given integrand above by a known convergent integrand (or below by a divergent one) to conclude. Example: bounding given integrand by 3/x^2 for large x to show convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated (two-sided) comparison (absolute-dominance) variant
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is nonnegative and for all x, |f(x)| ≤ g(x), and ∫_a^∞ g converges, then ∫_a^∞ f converges (i.e., dominated convergence in this elementary setting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the elementary (absolute domination) version: integrability of a dominating nonnegative function implies integrability of the dominated function. Use when f changes sign but is bounded in absolute value by a convergent positive integrand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail (Cauchy) test for convergence of improper integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of tail integrals ∫_{x_m}^{x_n} g can be made arbitrarily small for large m,n: if for every ε>0 there is B such that for all b≥B we have ∫_b^∞ g < ε, then the sequence of partial integrals is Cauchy and converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs of uniqueness of limits and to show convergence by bounding tails. The book uses this to show the sequence ∫_a^{x_n} f is Cauchy when dominated by a convergent g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: cannot split an improper integral arbitrarily
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not valid in general to split an improper integral into separate improper integrals and treat their limits independently; you cannot 'split the limit' unless each piece's limit exists appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: naive splitting that leads to '∞ - ∞' nonsense. You must verify each piece converges (or use definitions that justify the split).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: improper integral with two infinite endpoints (double limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on every bounded interval (a,b) and a, b are extended endpoints (±∞), define ∫_{-∞}^∞ f = lim_{A→-∞} lim_{B→∞} ∫_A^B f if the limits exist (with the convention of taking one endpoint limit for fixed other endpoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must be careful about the order of limits; the definition fixes an order (take d→b or ∞ for fixed c, etc.). The text emphasizes vigilance with double limits and prescribes taking one limit for fixed other endpoint, then the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-independence when both one-sided limits converge (Proposition 5.5.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is integrable on every bounded interval, then ∫_{-∞}^∞ f (defined as lim_{A→-∞} lim_{B→∞} ∫_A^B f) converges iff the reversed order lim_{B→∞} lim_{A→-∞} ∫_A^B f converges, and in that case the two values are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus when the iterated one-sided limits both exist, order can be interchanged and the improper integral value is well-defined. The proof uses splitting the integral at 0 and taking limits on each piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: independent asymmetric limits can mislead (counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if for each fixed A the limit as B→∞ of ∫_A^B f exists (and vice versa), the two-sided improper integral may still not exist; one must check the full double-limit convergence, not assume symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: a function with odd-symmetric behavior that produces infinite one-sided integrals but symmetric cancellation leads to principal-value-like behavior. The example shows the need to test convergence, not rely on partial behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy principal value (p.v.)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f integrable on (a,b) with a<c<b, define p.v. ∫_a^b f = lim_{ε→0+} (∫_a^{c-ε} f + ∫_{c+ε}^b f) if the limit exists. For infinite symmetric endpoints, p.v. ∫_{-∞}^∞ f = lim_{R→∞} ∫_{-R}^R f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal value assigns a value in some cases where the usual improper integral does not converge (e.g., odd integrands symmetric about 0 yield p.v.=0). Warning: principal value is a different notion and need not agree with (or imply) absolute convergence; use with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example / phenomenon: conditional convergence (sinc function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sinc function sinc(x)=sin x / x has ∫_{-∞}^∞ sinc(x) dx = π (convergent), but ∫_{-∞}^∞ |sinc(x)| dx diverges (non-absolutely convergent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates conditional convergence for integrals: convergence may occur without absolute integrability. The text shows how to prove convergence by subdividing into intervals and using alternating-area bounds rather than straightforward comparison to an absolutely integrable function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral test for series (Proposition 5.5.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : [k,∞) → ℝ is a decreasing nonnegative function, then ∑_{n=k}^∞ f(n) converges iff ∫_k^∞ f(x) dx converges. Moreover, bounds relate the sum and integral (partial-sum bounds via integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the integral test to determine convergence of positive-term series; the text provides inequalities bounding the series by integrals (and vice versa) useful for error estimates. Example: p-series with p=2 is shown to converge and used to bound the sum to within a target precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of integrals to bound series tails (error control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral test gives explicit bounds: ∑_{n=k}^∞ f(n) is between ∫_{k}^∞ f(x) dx + f(k) and ∫_{k-1}^∞ f(x) dx (or similar inequalities), allowing estimation of tails and partial sums to desired precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: choose k large enough so the integral tail is below desired ε to control the error of finite partial sums. Example: estimating ∑ 1/n^2 to within 0.01 using the integral remainder bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: pointwise convergence of functions (Definition 6.1.1 / Prop 6.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence f_n : S→ℝ converges pointwise to f if for every x∈S we have lim_{n→∞} f_n(x) = f(x). Equivalently: for every x and every ε>0 there exists N (depending on x) s.t. for all n≥N, |f_n(x)-f(x)|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key feature: N may depend on x. Many pathological examples show pointwise limits need not preserve continuity or integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: uniform convergence (Definition 6.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: f_n converges uniformly to f on S if for every ε>0 there exists N (independent of x) such that for all n≥N and all x∈S, |f_n(x)-f(x)|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence is stronger than pointwise and allows many limit operations (passing limits inside integrals, derivatives under extra hypotheses, continuity). The text emphasizes the dependence (or independence) of N on x as the dividing line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence (Proposition 6.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n → f uniformly on S, then f_n → f pointwise on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of definitions; used as a foundational fact when choosing hypotheses to interchange limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform norm / sup norm characterization (Definition 6.1.9 & Prop 6.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounded f on S define ||f||_S = sup_{x∈S} |f(x)|. A sequence f_n converges uniformly to f iff ||f_n - f||_S → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a concise metric viewpoint: uniform convergence = convergence in the sup norm. Useful for Cauchy/complete-space arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Cauchy criterion and completeness (Definition 6.1.12 & Proposition 6.1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence is Cauchy in uniform norm if for every ε>0 there exists N such that for all m,k≥N we have ||f_m - f_k||_S < ε. A sequence is uniformly Cauchy iff it converges uniformly to some bounded f (the space is complete under sup norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to show existence of uniform limits when you can establish uniform Cauchy behaviour. The proof constructs pointwise limits and upgrades to uniform convergence via the Cauchy bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence preserves continuity (Theorem 6.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S⊂ℝ and f_n are continuous on S and f_n → f uniformly on S, then f is continuous on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard interchange-of-limits result for continuity: uniform convergence allows passing the limit inside the evaluation limit along sequences and preserves continuity. Example and counterexample: a sequence of continuous functions that only converges pointwise may have a discontinuous limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence permits interchange of limit and integral (principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are integrable (on a fixed bounded interval) and converge uniformly to f, then the integral of the limit equals the limit of the integrals: ∫ lim f_n = lim ∫ f_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text illustrates failure when only pointwise convergence is assumed (example where integrals do not commute with pointwise limits). Uniform convergence is the typical sufficient condition used in elementary analysis courses; more general dominated-convergence-type theorems exist in measure theory.
